<|det|>text [86, 170, 912, 232]<|/det|>Description: Coordination between two malicious accounts combined with various other attack vectors fully documented in separate findings can be leveraged by an attacker to engineer scenarios in which liquidators are disincentivised or otherwise unable to unwind liquidatable positions due to an inability to recover the underlying collateral to which they are entitled.
<|det|>text [88, 238, 496, 254]<|/det|>To summarise the issues that make this attack possible:

<|det|>text [114, 329, 910, 375]<|/det|>- Incorrect accounting causes transfer amounts to become inflated for positions that were previously partially unwrapped. This can cause liquidation to revert as the violator will have insufficient ERC-6909 to complete the transfer.
<|det|>text [114, 381, 910, 413]<|/det|>- Enabling collateral for which the sender has no ERC-6909 balance can be similarly utilized to block successful transfer of other collateral assets against which the violator has borrowed vault assets.
<|det|>text [88, 420, 325, 435]<|/det|>Consider the following scenario:
<|det|>text [114, 442, 543, 458]<|/det|>- Alice and Bob are controlled by the same malicious user.
<|det|>text [114, 465, 843, 481]<|/det|>- Alice owns a position represented by tokenId1 and Bob owns a position represented by tokenId2.
<|det|>text [114, 488, 553, 503]<|/det|>- Both tokenId1 and tokenId2 positions accrue some fees.
<|det|>text [114, 510, 495, 524]<|/det|>- Alice transfers a small portion of tokenId1 to Bob.
<|det|>text [114, 532, 490, 547]<|/det|>- Bob performs a small partial unwrap of tokenId1.
<|det|>text [114, 555, 592, 570]<|/det|>- Both tokenId1 and tokenId2 positions accrue some more fees.
<|det|>text [114, 577, 701, 593]<|/det|>- Alice borrows the max debt and shortly after the position becomes liquidatable.
<|det|>text [114, 600, 910, 631]<|/det|>- Bob front-runs partial liquidation of tokenId1 with full unwrap of tokenId2 through partial unwrap (fee theft exploit).
<|det|>text [114, 638, 701, 654]<|/det|>- Partial liquidation succeeds, transferring a portion of tokenId1 to the liquidator.
<|det|>text [114, 660, 910, 691]<|/det|>- Liquidator attempts to partially unwrap tokenId1 to retrieve the underlying principal collateral plus fees but it reverts.
<|det|>text [114, 698, 910, 730]<|/det|>- This either causes a loss to the liquidator if executed in separate transactions or prevents/disincentivizes partial liquidation if executed atomically.
<|det|>text [114, 736, 704, 752]<|/det|>- The position continues to become undercollateralized until it is fully liquidatable.
<|det|>text [114, 758, 910, 789]<|/det|>- The transfer during liquidation will revert due to the transfer inflation issue calculating a transfer amount larger than Alice's balance.
<|det|>text [114, 796, 647, 812]<|/det|>- Alice's position is undercollateralized and bad debt accrues in the vault.

<|det|>text [86, 170, 912, 232]<|/det|>Description: Coordination between two malicious accounts combined with various other attack vectors fully documented in separate findings can be leveraged by an attacker to engineer scenarios in which liquidators are disincentivised or otherwise unable to unwind liquidatable positions due to an inability to recover the underlying collateral to which they are entitled.
<|det|>text [88, 238, 496, 254]<|/det|>To summarise the issues that make this attack possible:
<|det|>text [114, 261, 910, 322]<|/det|>- Fee theft causes partial unwraps to revert for positions that were already partially unwrapped. The expectation is that partial liquidation will execute and liquidator will perform a partial unwrap to recover the underlying collateral; however, this will not be possible if the wrapper contract holds insufficient balance to process the proportional transfer.
<|det|>text [114, 329, 910, 375]<|/det|>- Incorrect accounting causes transfer amounts to become inflated for positions that were previously partially unwrapped. This can cause liquidation to revert as the violator will have insufficient ERC-6909 to complete the transfer.
<|det|>text [114, 381, 910, 413]<|/det|>- Enabling collateral for which the sender has no ERC-6909 balance can be similarly utilized to block successful transfer of other collateral assets against which the violator has borrowed vault assets.
<|det|>text [88, 420, 325, 435]<|/det|>Consider the following scenario:
<|det|>text [114, 442, 543, 458]<|/det|>- Alice and Bob are controlled by the same malicious user.
<|det|>text [114, 465, 843, 481]<|/det|>- Alice owns a position represented by tokenId1 and Bob owns a position represented by tokenId2.
<|det|>text [114, 488, 553, 503]<|/det|>- Both tokenId1 and tokenId2 positions accrue some fees.
<|det|>text [114, 510, 495, 524]<|/det|>- Alice transfers a small portion of tokenId1 to Bob.
<|det|>text [114, 532, 490, 547]<|/det|>- Bob performs a small partial unwrap of tokenId1.
<|det|>text [114, 555, 592, 570]<|/det|>- Both tokenId1 and tokenId2 positions accrue some more fees.
<|det|>text [114, 577, 701, 593]<|/det|>- Alice borrows the max debt and shortly after the position becomes liquidatable.
<|det|>text [114, 600, 910, 631]<|/det|>- Bob front-runs partial liquidation of tokenId1 with full unwrap of tokenId2 through partial unwrap (fee theft exploit).
<|det|>text [114, 638, 701, 654]<|/det|>- Partial liquidation succeeds, transferring a portion of tokenId1 to the liquidator.
<|det|>text [114, 660, 910, 691]<|/det|>- Liquidator attempts to partially unwrap tokenId1 to retrieve the underlying principal collateral plus fees but it reverts.
<|det|>text [114, 698, 910, 730]<|/det|>- This either causes a loss to the liquidator if executed in separate transactions or prevents/disincentivizes partial liquidation if executed atomically.
<|det|>text [114, 736, 704, 752]<|/det|>- The position continues to become undercollateralized until it is fully liquidatable.
<|det|>text [114, 758, 910, 789]<|/det|>- The transfer during liquidation will revert due to the transfer inflation issue calculating a transfer amount larger than Alice's balance.
<|det|>text [114, 796, 647, 812]<|/det|>- Alice's position is undercollateralized and bad debt accrues in the vault.
<|det|>text [114, 819, 910, 865]<|/det|>- Note: without the transfer issue, Alice's entire tokenId balance is transferred to the liquidator, but still it is not possible to recover the underlying collateral even with full unwrap as the liquidator does not own the entire ERC-6909 supply (Bob still holds a small portion).

<|det|>text [87, 247, 912, 279]<|/det|>This is achieved by ERC721WrapperBase::transfer which allows the caller to specify the amount to transfer in terms of the underlying collateral value:
<|det|>text [92, 286, 905, 616]<|/det|>/// Notice For regular EVK vaults, it transfers the specified amount of vault shares from the sender to
    ↦ the receiver
    /// Vdev For ERC721WrapperBase, transfers a proportional amount of ERC8909 tokens (calculated as
    ↦ totalSupply(tokenId) * amount / balanceOf(sender)) for each enabled tokenId from the sender to the
    ↦ receiver.
    /// Vdev no need to check if sender is being liquidated, sender can choose to do this at any time
    /// Vdev when calculating how many ERC8909 tokens to transfer, rounding is performed in favor of the
    ↦ sender (typically the violator).
    /// Vdev This means that the sender may end up with a slightly larger amount of ERC8909 tokens than
    ↦ expected, as the rounding is done in their favor.
function transfer(address => uint256 amount) external callThroughEVC returns (bool) {
    address sender = _msgSender();
    uint256 currentBalance = balanceOf(sender);

    uint256 totalTokenIds = totalTokenIdsEnabledBy(sender);

    for (uint256 i = 0; i < totalTokenIds; ++i) {
    uint256 tokenId = tokenIdOfOwnerByIndex(sender, i);
    _transfer(sender, to, tokenId, normalizedToFull(tokenId, amount, currentBalance)); //this
    ← concludes the liquidation. The liquidator can come back to do whatever they want with the
    ← ERC6909 tokens
    }
    return true;
}
<|det|>text [87, 630, 910, 722]<|/det|>Here, balanceOf(sender) returns the sum value of each tokenId in uintOfAccount terms which is in turn used by normalizedToFull() to calculate the proportional amount of each ERC-6909 token enabled as collateral by the sender that should be transferred. These calculations work as intended when a sender owns the total ERC-6909 token supply for a given tokenId; however, this breaks if the sender owns less than 100% of a given tokenId and results in the corresponding calculations of ERC-6909 tokens to transfer being larger than they should be. This ultimately leads to the liquidator extracting more value in uintOfAccount than requested.
<|det|>text [88, 728, 550, 743]<|/det|>The source of this error is in the normalizedToFull() function:
<|det|>text [92, 750, 887, 822]<|/det|>function normalizedToFull(uint256 tokenId, uint256 amount, uint256 currentBalance) public view returns
    → (uint256) {
    // @audit => multiplying by the total ERC-6909 supply of the specified tokenId is incorrect
    return Math.mulDiv(amount, totalSupply(tokenId), currentBalance);
}
<|det|>text [87, 835, 908, 867]<|/det|>Here, the total supply of ERC-6909 tokens of the specified tokenId is erroneously used in the multiplication when this should instead be normalized to the actual amount of ERC-6909 tokens owned by the user.
<|det|>text [87, 873, 910, 920]<|/det|>Impact: More value can be extracted by liquidations than expected, causing the liquidated accounts to incur larger losses. This can occur by repeated partial liquidation or in the scenario a borrower transfers a portion of their position to a separate account.
